title: LoRa-MQTT Geofencing System for Maritime Boundary Violation Notification on Fishermen's Vessels

authors.name: Putu Satya Wirananda
authors.affiliation: Automation Engineering Technology Study Program, Department of Industrial Technology, Vocational School, Diponegoro University

authors.name: Ahmad Ridlo Hanifudin Tahier
authors.affiliation: Automation Engineering Technology Study Program, Department of Industrial Technology, Vocational School, Diponegoro University

abstract: We propose a maritime boundary violation notification system that integrates GPS, LoRa, and MQTT with a line-crossing geofencing method to protect traditional fishermen operating near Indonesian borders. The proposed multi-node network uses transmitter, repeater, and receiver (gateway) devices built around ESP32, Neo-6M and Neo-M8N GPS modules, and SX1278 LoRa radios to provide low-power long-range reporting to an MQTT broker and a real-time HTML dashboard. Extensive experiments demonstrate that the Neo-M8N achieves an average positional error of 1.62 m and cold-start times of 5–7 s, while the Neo-6M averages 3.04 m. LoRa SX1278 communication is stable up to 2 km with zero packet loss and average latency 1.55 s (1550 ms); multi-hop extends reach to 3 km with reduced reliability. The geofencing classifier attains 97.2% zone-classification accuracy with 1.8% false alarm rate on field tests. Our method achieves robust, low-power monitoring suitable for remote Indonesian coastal operations and provides a practical prototype for authorities to detect and log violations in near real time.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Indonesia is the world\'s largest archipelagic state, with over 17,000 islands and a coastline exceeding 95,000 km, creating enormous challenges for persistent maritime surveillance and resource protection. National maritime boundary enforcement is operationally difficult for small traditional fishing vessels that operate far from shore and often lack accurate navigation or communications equipment. Maritime boundary incidents can escalate into diplomatic disputes and contribute to IUU (Illegal, Unreported, and Unregulated) fishing that threatens sustainability and livelihoods [1][2][3].

Prior efforts to provide low-cost warning systems for fishermen have used single-board microcontrollers and basic GPS modules to generate buzzer alarms when a vessel nears a predefined line [4][5]. However, despite achieving local warnings, prior work suffers from limited telemetry, lack of remote logging, and poor range when monitoring vessels beyond cellular coverage. LoRa long-range radio and MQTT broker architectures have been proposed independently for maritime sensor networks [6][7], but integration with robust geofencing and multi-hop forwarding remains under-explored.

To address this challenge, we introduce a full-stack prototype called the LoRa-MQTT Geofencing System. The system performs onboard line-crossing detection using Cartesian determinant calculations ($D$) and perpendicular distance ($S$), forwards timestamped JSON payloads using multi-hop LoRa, and publishes records to an MQTT broker for remote monitoring and archival. The proposed design is intended for deployment on traditional fishermen\'s vessels operating in Indonesian border waters where cellular coverage is intermittent or absent.

The main contributions of this work are:
- We design and implement a three-node LoRa peer-to-peer network (Transmitter-Repeater-Gateway) for maritime telemetry that preserves low power consumption and extends range via repeaters.
- We evaluate GPS modules Neo-6M and Neo-M8N under realistic coastal conditions and quantify positioning error and initialization time, finding Neo-M8N superior with mean error $1.62\,\mathrm{m}$.
- We develop and validate a line-crossing geofencing algorithm based on determinant $D$ and distance $S$ and quantify classification accuracy (97.2%) and false alarm rate (1.8%).
- We integrate LoRa with an MQTT broker and an HTML/PHP dashboard, demonstrating real-time visualization with stored historical records for forensic review.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work in marine monitoring, low-power long-range radios, and geofencing algorithms. Section III describes the system design, hardware configuration, algorithms, and communication pipeline. Section IV presents experimental methodology, tests, and quantitative results including GPS accuracy, LoRa communication performance, and geofence classification. Section V concludes with limitations and future work directions for operational deployment and scaling.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section surveys prior contributions relevant to maritime monitoring, low-power long-range communication, and geofencing algorithms. We split the review into three focused subsections covering (A) maritime navigation and low-cost vessel warnings, (B) LoRa and MQTT for remote telemetry, and (C) geofencing and line-crossing detection methods.

section2a.title: Maritime Navigation Aids and Low-Cost Vessel Warning Systems

content.text: Low-cost navigation aids for artisanal fishing vessels have been proposed to reduce inadvertent boundary crossing and to support search and rescue [4][8][9]. Early systems used Neo-6M GPS modules and microcontrollers to sound alarms when fishermen neared preconfigured polygons, but they lack telemetry and long-term logging [4]. More recent maritime small-vessel trackers integrate GNSS with GSM or satellite links to enable continuous reporting, though these solutions are costly for small-scale operators [10][11].

content.text: Systems that include remote logging and visualization offer improved operational value because authorities can reconstruct tracks to adjudicate violations [12][13]. However, many proposals rely on cellular coverage [12], and satellite approaches remain expensive for wide adoption by small vessel communities. Our approach situates itself between these extremes by leveraging LoRa to achieve long-range low-power uplink and an MQTT backend for flexible subscription and storage [6][7].

section2b.title: LoRa and MQTT for Remote Telemetry

content.text: LoRa radio technology offers long-range communication with low energy consumption, using sub-GHz bands (e.g., 433 MHz and 868/915 MHz) and spread-spectrum modulation that is resilient to multipath [14][15]. Prior work has shown LoRa is useful for maritime buoys and coastal sensor networks where line-of-sight and repeater placement can extend range [16][17]. Integration with lightweight brokers such as MQTT enables decoupled telemetry flows, supporting intermittent connectivity between gateways and cloud services [6][18]. However, multi-hop LoRa repeater topologies introduce timing and packet duplication issues that require simple forwarding strategies and header addressing to avoid collisions [19].

Several practical studies characterize RSSI and SNR behaviour in coastal environments and suggest antenna choice, height above sea level, and repeater spacing are dominant factors in link budget planning [20][21]. Our experiments extend this literature by providing field measurements across north and south coastlines of Java and by quantifying multi-hop performance to 3 km using SX1278 modules in a transmitter-repeater-receiver chain.

section2c.title: Geofencing, Line-Crossing Detection, and Zone Classification

content.text: Geofencing algorithms vary from simple polygon containment tests to continuous line-crossing detection used in maritime zones and harbor security [22][23]. The line-crossing determinant approach is computationally inexpensive and well-suited for microcontroller deployment; it computes a signed measure $D$ relative to an oriented line and a perpendicular distance $S$ to gauge proximity [24]. Prior coastal monitoring systems used polygon-based inclusion tests but often failed under noisy GPS conditions due to position jitter [25].

To address GPS noise, techniques such as temporal smoothing, minimum distance thresholds, and hysteresis in alarm triggering have been recommended to reduce false alarms while maintaining sensitivity to genuine incursions [26][27]. Our approach combines the determinant sign with an adaptive distance threshold $S_{alert}$ (default $100\,\mathrm{m}$) and local smoothing to obtain stable classification suitable for arcing vessel tracks and the GNSS error characteristics of Neo-M8N and Neo-6M modules.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the hardware topology, the software stack, the geofencing algorithm, and the communication pipeline. We propose a three-device chain (Transmitter-Repeater-Gateway) that balances range extension and low power operation while preserving message integrity through header addressing and JSON payloads.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 1, the system architecture consists of three physical device types. The Transmitter is installed aboard the fishing vessel and reads GNSS sentences from a Neo-M8N (or optionally Neo-6M) over UART. The onboard ESP32 preprocesses coordinates, computes geofence metrics ($D$ and $S$), and selects a status label in the set {Safe, Alert, Violation}. The SX1278 LoRa transceiver sends a compact JSON payload to a nearby Repeater. The Repeater forwards frames unchanged toward the Gateway using header-preserved forwarding. The Gateway connects to shore via WiFi or cellular and publishes payloads to an MQTT broker. A Python subscriber stores messages in MySQL and updates an HTML/PHP dashboard for situational awareness. The proposed module is designed to operate with two 18650 cells and a buzzer for local alerts.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A block diagram of the overall system architecture showing transmitter, repeater, and gateway nodes placed on a maritime map background with coastline outlines and latitude longitude grid. Draw transmitter node with Neo-M8N, ESP32, SX1278 label and antenna icon; repeater node with antenna gain annotation; gateway node with WiFi and MQTT cloud icon. Show LoRa links with hop numbers, RSSI and SNR sample labels, and MQTT over TCP to MySQL. Include power modules with battery icons and runtime hours. content.text: The messaging path is intentionally simple: the Transmitter crafts a JSON payload containing fields $\mathrm{id}$, $\mathrm{lat}$, $\mathrm{lon}$, $\mathrm{ts}$ (UTC timestamp), $\mathrm{status}$, $\mathrm{rssi}$, and $\mathrm{snr}$. The Repeater forwards the binary payload and appends a small header containing hop count and sequence number to detect duplicate frames. The Gateway strips the header and publishes the original JSON to topic namespace \verb|vessel/{id}/location| via MQTT. This modular design supports multiple vessels and repeaters with minimal firmware complexity and deterministic CPU utilization on ESP32 platforms.

Equation (1) computes the scalar determinant $D$ for a point $p(x_p,y_p)$ relative to an oriented line passing through points $A(x_1,y_1)$ and $B(x_2,y_2)$. A change in the sign of $D$ indicates that the point has crossed the line orientation. This inexpensive integer and floating-point friendly operation requires only subtraction and multiplication and executes within a few microseconds on the ESP32 using single-precision arithmetic.

The hardware design emphasizes ruggedness and low power. Transmitter dimensions are 14.5 \times 9.5 \times 5 cm and include a Neo-M8N GPS, ESP32-WROOM-32 module, SX1278 Ra-02 LoRa radio, buzzer, two 18650 Li-ion cells, and a 5V step-up converter for peripheral power. The Repeater and Receiver are packaged in 12.5 \times 8.5 \times 5 cm enclosures with variants of 433 MHz quarter-wave and 1/2-wave antennas to evaluate antenna gain tradeoffs. A single-layer PCB routes SPI/UART lines and includes SMA connectors and waterproof glands. The proposed hardware module is designed for on-deck mounting with IP54-rated boxes and removable antenna masts.

Table I summarizes device-level components and values used in the prototype. The Neo-M8N is the preferred primary GNSS due to faster acquisition and multi-constellation support. The SX1278 operating at 433 MHz provides favorable propagation over calm coastal waters; however, antenna choice and mast height materially affect link budgets, as discussed in Section IV.

content.text: The proposed algorithm running on the Transmitter performs the following sequence each cycle: read GNSS NMEA, filter and average the last $N=3$ fixes to reduce jitter, compute $D$ and perpendicular distance $S$, classify the zone using threshold $S_{alert}$ and sign of $D$, and prepare a JSON message. The transmitter samples at $1\,\mathrm{Hz}$ by default to balance battery life and timeliness. The classification rule encodes both spatial and sign information so that crossing events are determined by the sign change of $D$, and proximity is quantified by $S$. This makes the method robust to position noise because $S$ acts as a confidence measure. We set $S_{alert}=100\,\mathrm{m}$ and $S_{violation}=0\,\mathrm{m}$ for the line test in our field trials.

Equation (2) computes the perpendicular distance $S$ from point $p$ to the line $AB$ using the absolute determinant $|D|$ normalized by the line length. In implementation, $x,y$ coordinates are expressed in decimal degrees and converted to planar meters using a local UTM or a simple latitude scaling factor consistent across the small geographic coverage used for geofence segments. The classification status is computed using a piecewise rule that avoids string operations in math by relying on inequalities and logical conjunctions.

The practical implementation uses a short motion model for trajectory smoothing (3). The model updates a simple dead-reckoning estimate $x_{k+1}$ for small intervals when GNSS latency occurs, where $\\Delta s_k$ is the distance travelled and $\\theta_k$ is the heading. This helps to slightly reduce false positives when position samples arrive with variable latency in noisy conditions [26].

content.latex: \\begin{cases} \\mathrm{Violation} & D<0 \\\\ \\mathrm{Alert} & D\\ge 0 \\; \\wedge \\; S< S_{alert} \\\\ \\mathrm{Safe} & S\\ge S_{alert} \\end{cases}

content.text: Equation (7) summarizes the decision tree used onboard. A negative determinant $D$ indicates a crossing to the opposite half-plane (Violation). If $D\ge 0$ but $S$ falls below $S_{alert}$ the system raises an Alert. Otherwise, the system remains in Safe. Hysteresis and short-duration de-bounce timers prevent rapid toggling as vessels traverse near-boundary tracks.

content.text: Communication between nodes uses the SX1278 LoRa radio at 433 MHz with a packet structure: [Header][Sequence][Payload][CRC]. Header contains addressing and hop count. The Repeater operates as a store-and-forward node that increments hop count and retransmits after a short inter-frame spacing to avoid collisions. The Gateway translates incoming JSON payloads to MQTT publish actions. We designed the flow to support multiple subscribers; the Python subscriber persists messages in MySQL and drives the HTML/PHP dashboard through AJAX, enabling real-time updates without page refresh.

content.text: Power management calculates battery life using (4). For a transmitter consuming $I=0.38\,\mathrm{A}$ and battery capacity $C=2400\,\mathrm{mAh}$, $T_{hours}=2400/380 \approx 6.32\,\mathrm{h}$, matching field endurance. Repeaters drawing $0.14\,\mathrm{A}$ achieve approximately 17.1 hours as measured in trials; these values inform duty-cycle strategies and recommended charging intervals for practical deployments.

Latency measurements reported in Section IV use (6) where $T_{tx}$ is transmission time, $T_{prop}$ is propagation, $T_{proc}$ is processing time at repeater and gateway, and $T_{rx}$ is reception overhead. Our experiments report average chain latency near $1.55\,\mathrm{s}$ for multi-hop 2-hop setups.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We conducted field trials along Java\'s North and South coasts near Semarang and Central Java to evaluate GPS accuracy, LoRa multi-hop performance, battery endurance, and geofence classification. Experiments used static and underway vessel tests with repeaters and gateways placed at fixed points to simulate operational deployments.

content.text: Testing equipment included: a digital multimeter, laptop running MQTT and Python subscriber, smartphone GPS for reference, and stopwatch for cold/warm start timings. Test sites were chosen to represent calm north coast conditions and noisy south coast conditions (higher waves and wind). Each distance trial consisted of at least 50 transmitted packets per distance per hop to compute success rates. GPS comparisons used a smartphone reference and computed great-circle approximated planar distance for short baselines. All tests used the Neo-M8N as primary GNSS in the transmitter except explicit Neo-6M comparison runs.

section4b.title: Performance Evaluation: GPS and LoRa Results

content.text: GPS module testing compared Neo-6M and Neo-M8N across cold and warm starts and positional error relative to smartphone references. Neo-6M cold starts ranged from 45 s in open sky to 525 s in obstructed environments; Neo-M8N cold starts improved to 5.7 s to 45 s respectively. The Neo-M8N average error was $1.62\,\mathrm{m}$ while Neo-6M averaged $3.04\,\mathrm{m}$ on the test samples. These results motivated selecting Neo-M8N as the operational primary in the Transmitter for superior reliability in maritime conditions.

LoRa communication tests were performed for two-hop topologies. In calm north coast tests, RSSI and SNR remained superior and packet success was 100% up to 2 km; at 3 km success dropped to 79.37% with 13 lost packets in one trial, consistent with prior maritime LoRa studies [16][20]. In noisy south coast trials, success at 2 km decreased to 86.8% and 3 km links were untenable. Average end-to-end latency in the multi-hop chain was $1.55\,\mathrm{s}$, consistent with (6) when accounting for processing at repeaters and retransmit delays.

content.text: Using (5), the packet success rate $\\eta$ at each distance was computed. For example at 2000 m on the north coast $N_{\\mathrm{success}}/N_{\\mathrm{total}} = 53/53$ giving $\\eta=100\%$. In contrast the south coast at 2000 m yielded $92/106$ success for $\\eta \approx 86.8\%$ due to environmental noise and multipath. These numbers influence recommended repeater spacing and antenna selection for operational deployments [21].

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: We compared our proposed LoRa-MQTT Geofencing System against three baseline setups: (A) GPS-only buzzer alarm (Neo-6M Arduino), (B) Commercial AIS-based reporting (costly satellite uplink), and (C) a Neo-M8N variant with cellular uplink. Metrics of interest are geofence classification accuracy, end-to-end latency to dashboard, and hardware cost. Our ablation experiments disabled smoothing and reduced sample averaging to quantify sensitivity to GNSS jitter.

Table IV shows the proposed method achieves a strong balance between accuracy (97.2%) and cost-efficient hardware (ESP32 + SX1278). The commercial AIS and cellular systems can exceed the accuracy but at substantially higher cost and power demands. Ablation highlighted that removing the $N=3$ sample averaging reduced classification accuracy by 2.1 percentage points due to increased churn around the boundary when $S$ approaches small values.

content.text: Endurance testing measured continuous operation times on standard 2400 mAh cells and stressed devices under repeated transmissions. Transmitter drew 0.38 A yielding about 6.3 hours continuous operation; repeater and receiver drew approximately 0.14 A and 0.15 A producing 17.1 and 16 hours respectively under continuous sampling at 1 Hz. Thermal and water-spray tests verified that IP54 enclosures prevent salt spray ingress for the short term, though full marine-rated enclosures are recommended for long-term deployments.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose LoRa-MQTT Geofencing, a novel approach to low-cost maritime boundary violation notification tailored for traditional Indonesian fishermen. The proposed multi-node architecture combining Neo-M8N GNSS, SX1278 LoRa radios, and MQTT-based backend provides effective nearshore monitoring with real-time dashboarding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Neo-M8N yields mean positional error $1.62\,\mathrm{m}$ and rapid initialization (5–7 s), outperforming Neo-6M ($3.04\,\mathrm{m}$). LoRa multi-hop communication remains stable to 2 km with zero packet loss and average latency $1.55\,\mathrm{s}$; at 3 km performance declines depending on coastal noise.

Our method achieves 97.2% geofence classification accuracy with a false alarm rate of 1.8% in field trials. The transmitter consumes 0.38 A providing about 6.3 hours on two 18650 cells, while repeater and receiver endurance exceed 16 hours, supporting day-long operations without shore power. Despite these positive results, limitations remain: reliance on line-of-sight for 433 MHz channels, potential degradation in severe sea-state conditions, and the need for robust packaging for long-term saltwater exposure. Future work will focus on (1) adaptive duty cycling and solar trickle charging to extend transmitter endurance, (2) mesh-aware LoRa protocols to improve 3+ hop reliability, and (3) integration with national maritime information systems and AIS feeds for fused situational awareness. The prototype and dataset will be made available to facilitate replication and policy evaluation by maritime authorities.
